title: Nancy Duarte: How to Create Better Visual Presentations
transcript: [Music] A lot of times when we have a specific piece of communication that we need to do, we run over and we open up PowerPoint and we just start to think linearly. We are like, "Okay, slide one, slide this. I'm going to go grab six slides over here, two from this deck, two and we Frankenstein this thing together and we jump up and then we present." And we think that that's effective communication and it's not. In reality, what you need to do is think about your audience. just obsess about the audience and then think about stories and ways that you can make a heart-to-heart connection with them. Think through what the one big idea is you want to convey and then you build all the content around [Music] that. The most important thing to remember when you're building out your slides is contrast. You need to prioritize for the audience the order in which they're to process your information. So you got to think about how their eye is going to flow across the information. What's the most dominant thing? So what's primary? What's secondary? What's tertiary information? You can use colors to do that. You can use shapes to do that. But you need to simplify everything because if you think about the concept of contrast, you could think about its opposite, which would be camouflage. Right? Right now in slide decks, everything looks the same. There's not one dominant thing and there's not everything else secondary to that. So, if you think about camouflage and you look at every slide as if you're trying to minimize the amount of camouflage to your idea, you can actually find that one key thing that you're trying to do and just amplify that by using a big contrasting color or or making a really minimal color palette, making that one thing pop out. Um, it's really important that it pop the one idea. So, every slide should have one big idea and you need to make sure visually that that one big idea is amplified and not lost in the mire of your speaker notes. One of the things that's happened is we use PowerPoint uh two ways. Uh you could use it as a visual aid or a cinematic backdrop to support your idea when you're on stage presenting. But the other thing that's happened is it's become our visual document tool instead of people running out and getting these very expensive design programs. We're designing our documents incorporations in PowerPoint. But the FL and that's great. You could use it for your cinematic. You could use it for your um documents. But the problem is we're in this weird blurry in between thing where it's kind of this mix between a document, a teleprompter thing, and it's got tons of text. And then what happens is you show up to an audience, you turn your back to the audience, and you're hosting a read along. Well, the audience can read faster than you're spewing out the bullets, and they're thinking, "This guy's an idiot. I already know everything what he's saying because I already read ahead." Well, you don't want that to happen to you. So, you want to make sure you're either either using it as a visual aid or as a document. If you're choosing to put a ton of words on it and you're choosing to use it as a document, distribute it as a document. Talk about it as if it's a document, but don't stand up and present your documents to an audience. [Music]

title: TEDxEast - Nancy Duarte uncovers common structure of greatest communicators 11/11/2010
transcript: Translator: Sophia Kuchina Editor: Natalia Ost I am very glad to be here. You have the power to change the world. I don't want this to sound cliche, but you really can do it. Deep within you, each of you, is the most powerful instrument known to humanity. This tool is an idea. So, one idea in our minds can make a revolution, start a new movement, and it has real power to change our future. But an idea is powerless if it remains inside you. If this idea remains with you, inaccessible to others, it will die with you. Maybe some of you tried to pitch your idea but it was not accepted, it was rejected and some other mediocre idea was approved. And the only difference between them was how they were presented. Because if you express an idea in a way that resonates, change will happen and you can change the world. My family collects vintage European posters. Every time we go to Maui, we go to a local vendor and he puts out these awesome posters. I love them. Each one has one idea and one single image that conveys it. They are the size of a mattress - very large. Not as dense as a mattress, but they are large. The seller will tell you the story by turning the pages. At that time, I had my two children next to me, and he turns the page, and at the bottom is this poster. And at that moment, I leaned forward and said, “Oh my God! "How I love this poster!" — the children jumped back and exclaimed: “Oh my God! "Mom, it's you!" And here is this poster. (Laughter) See, it's like I'm saying, "Fire!" I liked the irony in this poster. Here's this beauty, all ready for battle, like a standard bearer, and she's holding these little baking spices like they're nothing, even though she's willing to give her life to advertise them. So if you replace those little baking spices with presentation... Yeah, I'm that excited. I was inspired by performing before it was considered cool. I truly believe they have the power to change the world if used effectively to communicate an idea. Changing the world is not easy. This won't happen if there is only one person with one idea. The idea must spread or it will have no effect. Therefore, it must come from you and be accessible to others. The most effective way to convey an idea is to tell a story. For thousands of years, illiterate people have been passing on their values ​​and culture to their descendants, intact and safe, from generation to generation. So there is something magical about the structure of a story that, once it is told, makes it easy for the listener to absorb and remember it. In general, a story being told evokes a physical reaction: your heart may beat faster, your eyes may widen, you may say, “Oh, I get goosebumps” or “I feel a little sick in the pit of my stomach. ” We react physically when someone tells us a story. So even if the scene doesn't change, you can tell a story, but the performance will be a complete failure. And I wanted to understand why. Why is it that we sit spellbound when listening to a story, but the same doesn't happen with a performance. So I wanted to understand how I could incorporate stories into my performances. We had thousands of presentations in that store, hundreds of thousands in fact. So I knew cases of really bad presentations. I decided to start by studying film and literature, to really delve into the subject and understand what was going on and why it didn't work that way. So, I want to show you some of my findings, which, as I found out, led to a specific form of performance. The obvious step was to start with Aristotle. He believed that structure consists of three parts: beginning, middle and end. We have studied poetics and rhetoric, and many speeches do not have this even in its most basic form. Then, when I moved on to studying hero archetypes, I thought, “Okay, the performer is the hero, he’s on stage, he’s the star of the show.” It's easy to feel like a star when giving a presentation. I immediately realized that it doesn't work that way. If I have an idea, I can share it, but if you don’t understand it, if it doesn’t touch you, then this idea will disappear and the world will never change. Therefore, in reality, the speaker is not the hero; the hero of our idea is the audience. If you look at Joseph Campbell's hero's journey, it was only at the beginning that there were really interesting ideas. There is a relatable hero in the mundane world who feels the call to adventure. And the world seems to lose harmony. At first the hero resists, he’s like, “I’m not sure I want to get involved in this.” And then a mentor comes and helps him to leave the ordinary world and enter a special world. And this is the role of the speaker - to be a mentor. You are not Luke Skywalker, you are Yoda. You are the one who truly helps the audience move from the initial state to your new and special idea. And that is the power of history. The simplest structure in the story is three parts. You have a compelling hero who has a desire, who faces an obstacle and is ultimately transformed— that's the basic structure. But that was until I came across Gustav Freytag's pyramid: he invented this figure in 1863. He was a German playwright... he was a German playwright and he believed in a five-part structure, which has an exposition, a plot, a climax, a resolution, and an ending where the story's problem is revealed or resolved. I like this figure. Let's talk about figures. There is an arc in history, and an arc is a figure. We say that classical music is well composed. So I thought, "If presentations had a shape, what would it be?" and “How did the greatest orators use this figure, and did they use it at all?” I will never forget it, it was Saturday morning. After all this research - two years of research - I drew a figure. And I was like, “Oh my god, if this figure exists, then I could take two completely different speeches and superimpose it on them and it would be true.” I took the obvious: I took Martin Luther King’s “I Have a Dream” speech and Steve Jobs’s speech at the presentation of the iPhone in 2007. I put a shape on them and it worked. I sat in my office, completely stunned. I even cried a little: “This is just a gift from above.” And here it is, here is the figure of a magnificent presentation. Is n't it wonderful? (Sobbing) (Laughter) I cried. I want to take you through it, it's quite amazing. There is a beginning, a middle and an end, and I want to walk you through it all. Because great speakers... I've gone through speeches and all that... I can really put on a figure. Even the Gettysburg Address fits it. At the beginning of any presentation you need to show what you have. You know, "this is the status quo, this is what's happening." And then you need to compare that to what could have been. You need to make this difference as big as possible, because there is the ordinariness of the status quo, and you need to show the grandeur of your idea in contrast. For example: “There is the past, there is the present, but look at our future.” "Here's a problem, but look how it disappears." "Here is an obstacle, let's destroy it." You need to really emphasize this difference. It works like a cliffhanger in a movie. And then the audience should suddenly be wondering about what you just laid out: “Wow, do I want to agree and come to terms with this or not?” And for the rest of the presentation, they should support this idea. In the middle, one can move back and forth and oscillate between what is and what could be, what is and what could be. You are trying to make the status quo and the norm unattractive and want to entice the audience with what could be in the future if your idea were accepted. People will resist your path to changing the world. They won't catch fire: they can love the world as it is. You will encounter resistance. So you have to move back and forth. It's like swimming. When you are sailing against the wind and the wind is resisting you need to steer the boat back and forth, back and forth. This way you can catch the wind. You need to catch the resistance directed against you as you swim. What's interesting is that if you catch the wind correctly and set your sail correctly, your boat will actually go faster than the wind itself. This is a physical phenomenon. When it comes to speaking up, having them disagree with what is and what could be will actually get them on board with your idea faster than if you didn't. After you've wavered between what is and what could be, the final turning point is the call to action, which should be in any presentation, but at the very end. You need to describe the world as a new hope. “This is the kind of utopia that will arise if my idea is accepted.” "This is what the world will look like when we come together and solve this serious problem." You need to use this as an ending in a very poetic and dramatic way. What's interesting is that when I finished, I thought, "You know what? I can use this for analysis." I actually transcribed speeches and worked out how they fit this pattern. I want to show some of them today. And I want to start with the people I took on first. Here is Mr. Jobs, who completely changed the world. It has changed the world of personal computers, the music industry, and is now on its way to changing the mobile device industry. He definitely changed the world. And here is the form of his speech in 2007, when he released his iPhone. It's a 90-minute speech, you can see how he starts with what is, moves back and forth, and ends with what could be. I want to take a closer look at this: the white line is where he speaks, his speech. The next colored line you'll see appear is where it breaks in the video. This way he adds variety by inserting his own video. So he doesn't do all the talking himself. These lines are clearly shown here. Towards the end you will see a blue line. This is a guest speaker. And this is where things get interesting: the checkmarks here are where he made everyone laugh. And every tick here is where he was applauded. The audience is physically involved in the presentation, they physically respond to what he says, and that's actually amazing because then you can be sure that you have the audience. He begins with what could have been: “I have been looking forward to this day for two and a half years.” He's launching a product he's known about for a couple of years. So this product is not new to him. But look at what he does: he admires. He admires his own product. He himself admires more than the audience laughs or applauds. It's like he's saying, 'Isn't it cool? "Is n't it wonderful?" He models for the audience the emotions he wants them to feel. Basically , he forces them to feel a certain way. Here he begins with what could have been: “Every now and then a revolutionary product comes along and changes everything.” He starts to go into detail and talks about his new product. At first he doesn't turn on the phone. And you can see that the line is mostly white up to this point, and it's oscillating between, "Here's this new phone, and here are the competitors that suck. Here's this new phone, and here are the crappy competitors." And then, at that moment, his moment of glory - and that is what we will always remember. He turns on the phone. The audience sees scrolling for the first time, you can hear the oxygen leaving the room. They gasped in amazement. This way he creates a moment that they will remember forever. If you move the model, you can see the blue color where the guest speakers enter, and the line breaks off towards the bottom right corner. It's because his remote control is broken. He wants to keep the excitement alive and tells a story from his personal life right at the point where technology failed. He is a master communicator and he tells a story to keep his audience engaged. At the top right he ends with new hope. He leaves them with the promise that Apple will continue to create revolutionary products. And he says, "There's an old Wayne Gretzky quote that I really love: 'I skate to where the puck is going to be, not where it's been.' We've tried to follow this from the very beginning at Apple and we always will." And he ends with a new utopia. Now let's look at Mr. King. He was a brilliant strategist and preacher who fought for equality throughout his life. And here is the form of his speech: “I have a dream.” You see, he starts with what is, moves from what is to what could be, and ends with a very poetic ideal, we all know that famous part. I'll enlarge this part a little and stretch it out for you. Here I have placed a transcript of the entire speech. I know you can't read this. But at the end of each line I made a break because he would take a breath and stop. A Southern Baptist preacher, most people had never heard anything like him before, so his pace and rhythm of speech were unfamiliar to people. I want to cover these lines with text with a stripe because I'm using it here for information. Let's go over how he actually spoke to people. The blue stripes here would indicate that he used the oratorical technique of repetition. He repeated himself, he used the same words and phrases so that people could remember and reproduce them. But he also used metaphors and imagery. It was a way to take very complex ideas and make them memorable and informative so that people would understand them. He actually created almost pictures with his words so that they could illustrate what he was saying. He also used many famous songs and Bible quotes. You see only the beginning. He also made many political references to the promises that were made to the people. If you look at the first time he spoke about what is, at the very end of what is, for the first time people really applauded and roared loudly. So, at the end of it all, he said, "America gave black people a bad check that came back marked 'insufficient funds.'" Everyone knows what it's like to have no money in your account. And he used a metaphor that is very close to people. But for the first time they really caught fire and really shouted at the words: “And we have come to cash this check, a check that will give us the treasures of freedom and the guarantees of justice.” Then they really applauded. Then he compared what we have now with what could be. If you move a little further into this pattern, you will see it moving back and forth at a more frantic pace. And then he starts walking back and forth, back and forth. The audience was already on edge by then. They were all excited, so you can use this to keep them excited. He says: "I have a dream that one day this nation will rise up and live up to its creed." "We hold to these truths to be an example that men are created equal." He uses a little orange text to remind them of the promise made to him by politicians and this country. Then he goes back and forth, "I have a dream that one day, I have a dream that one day, I have a dream that one day," and at the end it gets very interesting because he uses—look at the four shades of green, there's a lot of blue here, so he used a lot of repetition, he has a high level of repetition. And green means a high frequency of songs and biblical texts. So, the first batch of green is the actual texts from the Book of Prophet Isaiah. The second batch of green is "My country, it's about you." It's a famous song that was especially important to black people at the time because it was a song where they changed the words to a cry of despair, saying that promises were not kept. And the third batch of green is an excerpt from the song “My Country, It’s About You.” And the fourth is a spiritual song of African Americans. "Finally free! Finally free! Thank you, Lord, I am finally free! He, in essence, reached into the depths of the listeners' souls. He quoted sacred texts, and that's important. He selected excerpts from songs they sang together to protest against the breaking of the law, and he used all of this as a means of connecting and relating to the audience. In the end, he paints a picture of new hope, using that very thing within them that they already considered hidden. He was a great man and he had a great dream. There are a lot of people sitting here, and you all have really big dreams. There are truly great ideas within you that you need to share. But you know, we are facing difficulties. Changing the world is not easy – it is hard work. You know, he was... his house was bombed, they stuck a box cutter into it. In the end, he lost his life because he cared. But many of us won't have to make such sacrifices. What happens, though, is that it's a bit like the basic structure of a story. Life can be like this. You know, you are all nice people, you have desire, you face obstacles, and that's where we stop. We all do this: “I had an idea, but I’m not going to share it. She's already been rejected once." You know, we sabotage our own ideas, we just back away and back away from obstacles, instead of allowing difficulties to change us and go forward and implement this idea. And you know, if everyone... if I can do it, then everyone can. I grew up in an economically and emotionally impoverished environment. The first time I went to camp with my sister, I was abused. This was not the first case of violence, but it was the most aggressive. And my mom and dad... they married each other three times. (Mumbling) Yes, it was exciting, and when they weren't fighting, they were helping the alcoholics who lived with us sober up because they were both sober. My mother left us when I was 16. I looked after the house and my brothers and sisters. And I got married, I met a man. Fell in love. I studied at college for a year. I did everything a single, vibrant young woman should do: I got married when I was 18. And you know what? I knew, I knew that I was born for something more. And at that moment in my life I had a choice. I could have let it all crush me, let all my ideas die inside me. I could say that life is too complicated to change the world. It's just too heavy. But I chose a different story for my life. (Laughter) Don't know which one? I think there are people in this room... you have these little baking spices and you think, "You know, it's not that important. “ I can’t change the whole world.” But you know, you can change your world. You can change your life. You can change the world under your control, you can change your environment. I want to encourage you to do this. Because you know what? The future is not a place where we end up. This is the place we need to create. Thank you. Be healthy. (Applause)
